---
title: "Method"
subtitle: "How BF-NEE links natural ecosystem loss to agricultural production and final demand"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
library(knitr)
```

## Overview

BF-NEE combines three data sets that each play a distinct role:

| Data set | Role |
|---|---|
| **LandSHIFT** | Cropland extent per grid cell; crop composition per country |
| **GlobES** | Composition of ecosystem classes (IUCN habitat scheme) and its change |
| **GLORIA** (MRIO) | Share of each crop's production that ends up in German final demand |

The analysis covers the years 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010 and 2015 and therefore four
five-year periods. Each period $y-1 \rightarrow y$ is combined with the commodity and
GLORIA factors of its **end year** $y$.

## 1 · Harmonising cropland

LandSHIFT is the authoritative source for cropland. In every grid cell the GlobES
agricultural classes (14.1 arable land, 15.8 seasonally flooded agricultural land)
are rescaled to the LandSHIFT cropland fraction $L_{p,y}$, and all other classes are
rescaled so that the cell still sums to one. Six anthropogenic classes (14.4, 14.5,
15.4, 15.5, 15.6, 15.11) are removed beforehand.

::: {.equation-box}
$$
\sum_{a \in A} G'_{p,a,y} = L_{p,y}, \qquad \sum_e G'_{p,e,y} = 1, \qquad
A_{p,e,y} = G'_{p,e,y}\,A_p
$$
:::

## 1b · Intensive pasture  {#pasture}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Since v3.** Intensive pasture is part of the agricultural land.
:::

LandSHIFT assigns a grazing fraction to every cell with livestock, both
**intensive** pastures and **extensive** grazing on natural vegetation such as
savanna. LandSHIFT separates the two only by stocking density, using the
country mean as the threshold. BF-NEE follows this with **one fixed threshold
per country**: the mean stocking density of the grazing land in 1995–2015,
weighted by grazing area. A cell's grazing fraction counts as intensive pasture
$L^{past}_{p,y}$ if its stocking density is above that threshold. Extensive grazing
stays part of the natural GlobES cover.

GlobES is coupled to both agricultural land uses separately:

::: {.equation-box}
$$
\sum_{a \in \{14.1,\,15.8\}} G'_{p,a,y} = L^{crop}_{p,y}, \qquad
G'_{p,14.2,y} = L^{past}_{p,y}, \qquad
G'_{p,e,y} = \tilde G_{p,e,y}\,\frac{1 - L^{crop}_{p,y} - L^{past}_{p,y}}{1 - \tilde G^{crop}_{p,y} - \tilde G^{past}_{p,y}}
$$
:::

Pastureland (14.2) is therefore an agricultural class and no longer counted as natural.

## 2 · Loss of natural ecosystems

For every natural ecosystem class $e$ the gross loss between two observations is

::: {.equation-box}
$$
\text{Loss}_{p,e,y} = \max\!\left(-\Delta A_{p,e,y},\,0\right), \qquad
N_{p,y} = \sum_{e \in N} \text{Loss}_{p,e,y}
$$
:::

Expansion of one natural class does not offset the loss of another.

## 3 · Agricultural-expansion constraint

Not every ecosystem change is caused by agriculture. Only loss that coincides with
a **net increase of agricultural land (cropland + intensive pasture) in the same grid
cell and period** is attributed. Pasture converted to cropland is not counted as
expansion:

::: {.equation-box}
$$
\text{Gain}^{agri}_{p,y} = \max\!\left(\Delta A^{crop}_{p,y} + \Delta A^{past}_{p,y},\,0\right), \qquad
R_{p,y} = \min\!\left(N_{p,y},\ \text{Gain}^{agri}_{p,y}\right)
$$
:::

$R$ is split in every cell into a cropland and a pasture part in proportion to the
positive changes of the two land uses:

::: {.equation-box}
$$
s^{past}_{p,y} = \frac{\max(\Delta A^{past}_{p,y},0)}{\max(\Delta A^{crop}_{p,y},0) + \max(\Delta A^{past}_{p,y},0)}, \qquad
R^{past}_{p,y} = s^{past}_{p,y} R_{p,y}, \quad R^{crop}_{p,y} = (1 - s^{past}_{p,y}) R_{p,y}
$$
:::

## 4 · Keeping the ecosystem classes  {#class-split}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Since v2.** Previously the constraint was applied to the total $N_{p,y}$ only,
so the information on *which* ecosystem was lost disappeared.
:::

The constrained loss $R_{p,y}$ is split onto the ecosystem classes in proportion to
their original loss in the same cell:

::: {.equation-box}
$$
R_{p,e,y} =
\begin{cases}
R_{p,y}\,\dfrac{\text{Loss}_{p,e,y}}{N_{p,y}} & N_{p,y} > 0\\[4pt]
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \sum_e R_{p,e,y} = R_{p,y}
$$
:::

*Example:* a cell loses 10 km² forest and 5 km² savanna, but cropland grows by only
6 km². Then 4 km² are attributed to forest and 2 km² to savanna. Footprints for
forests, savannas, wetlands or tropical moist forests therefore add up exactly to
the total footprint.

## 5 · Commodity shares from expansion  {#commodity-shares}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Since v2.** Previously the *static* share of each crop in total cropland was used.
:::

Ecosystems are converted by crops that **expand**, not by fields that already exist.
For each country and period, the share of crop $c$ is its area increase relative to
the summed increase of all expanding crops:

::: {.equation-box}
$$
S_{c,r,y} =
\frac{\max\!\left(A_{c,r,y} - A_{c,r,y-1},\,0\right)}
     {\sum_{c'} \max\!\left(A_{c',r,y} - A_{c',r,y-1},\,0\right)}
$$
:::

Crops whose area shrank get $S = 0$; the shares of a period sum to one. If no crop
expanded, all shares are zero and nothing is attributed.

## 6 · Attribution and indicator

The cropland part is attributed to crops with the commodity share and the GLORIA
production share $P_{c,r,y}$ (share of production in country $r$ that is used for
German final demand). The pasture part is attributed to *Grazing livestock*, whose
$P^{past}$ is the mean of the GLORIA sectors *Raising of cattle* and *Raising of sheep
and goats*:

::: {.equation-box}
$$
L_{p,e,c,y} = R^{crop}_{p,e,y}\,S_{c,r,y}\,P_{c,r,y}, \qquad
L_{p,e,past,y} = R^{past}_{p,e,y}\,P^{past}_{r,y}, \qquad
\text{BF-NEE}_y = \sum_p \sum_e \Big(\sum_c L_{p,e,c,y} + L_{p,e,past,y}\Big)
$$
:::

Summing $L_{p,e,c,y}$ over any subset gives the footprint of that subset – e.g. of
one ecosystem group, one country or one commodity. All values are areas in km².

## Ecosystem groups

For the website the IUCN classes are grouped as follows. *Tropical moist forest* is
reported additionally (classes 1.6 and 1.9; it is part of *Forest*).

```{r}
lookup <- read_csv("data/lookup/ecosystem_classes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                   col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

lookup %>%
  group_by(`Group` = eco_group) %>%
  summarise(`IUCN classes` = paste(ecosystem_class, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Group = factor(Group, levels = eco_group_levels)) %>%
  arrange(Group) %>%
  kable()
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Note on modified habitats.** Since v3, pastureland (14.2) is agricultural land.
Plantations (14.3), heavily degraded former forest (14.6) and several artificial
aquatic classes are still **not** excluded and therefore count as "natural". They
are shown as a separate group so they can be judged – or excluded – explicitly.
:::

## Limitations

- Commodity and GLORIA factors are national, not pixel-specific: the indicator does
  not identify the crop planted on a specific converted pixel.
- The constraint is spatially conservative – loss is attributed only where cropland
  grows in the same cell and five-year period. Transitions that happen and reverse
  between snapshots are not captured.
- Only intensive pasture is agricultural land; the split between intensive and extensive
  grazing depends on the country-mean threshold. Cattle and sheep/goats are weighted
  equally in $P^{past}$ (no per-cell information on species).
- The LandSHIFT–GLORIA concordance is not one-to-one (e.g. pulses and oil crops share
  one GLORIA sector).
